items.title: An Evidence-Grounded Framework for Evaluating AI-Generated Educational Feedback
items.abstract: Educational feedback generated by artificial intelligence is becoming more and more popular in teaching, but there are still differences in how to evaluate its quality in existing research. This study examined 68 empirical studies and compared the criteria, methods, evaluators, and evidence used in these evaluations. The results show that the relevant evaluation can be roughly summarised into three dimensions: Evidence Validity, Rubric and Task Alignment, and Pedagogical Usefulness. Evidence Validity focuses on whether the feedback is accurate and reliable, and is based on the learner's actual work. Rubric and Task Alignment focuses on whether the feedback meets the task requirements, evaluation criteria, and learner responses. Pedagogical Usefulness focuses on whether the feedback is clear, specific, actionable, and can support revision and further learning. The reviewed studies also used a variety of evidence to judge the quality of feedback, including human judgement, learner perceptions, revision behaviour, learning outcomes, and automated metrics. Based on these findings, this study proposes an evaluation framework that links different dimensions of feedback quality with corresponding evidence to provide clearer evaluation ideas for subsequent research and educational practice.

items.title: Artificial Emotional Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Emotional Intelligence (AEI) refers to Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that mediate human affect by sensing, processing, and responding to emotional states through multimodal inputs, including text, voice, and physiological signals (Chen et al. 2024 ). As AI systems (especially generative AI) become more conversational, personalised, and multimodal, AEI increasingly mediates therapy, companionship, customer service, education, and work (De Freitas et al. 2026 ; Zao-Sanders 2026 ). This marks a shift from mediating information and behaviour to mediating affect in sensitive contexts: AEI already underpins chatbots designed to mitigate suicide risk (Maples et al. 2024 ), customer-service systems that respond to frustration (Fan et al. 2024 ), and personalised sexbot applications (Rubinsztein and Ciriello 2024 ). This shift reflects technical progress, but also intensifies concerns about social fragmentation, care-capacity gaps, and the expansion of monetisation-oriented platform logics into domains historically organised around care, trust, and professional duty (Arsel 2026 ; Leong et al. 2021 ; Seleznova et al. 2023 ). Despite its significance, this reconfiguration of digital intermediation remains under-conceptualised in Information Systems (IS) research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Job Design: A Dynamic Framework
items.abstract: This study aims to deepen the understanding of artificial intelligence's (AI) impact on work by introducing and describing the AI-Job Dynamics Framework. Drawing from sociotechnical systems theory, complexity theory, and organizational learning theories, we conceptualize AI integration as a dynamic, non-linear process with three key phases. The framework, supported by theoretical propositions, identifies how this process affects organizational decision-making structures and key job characteristics over time, emphasizing the balance between centralization and decentralization of decision-making power. AI integration initially reduces job autonomy but may lead to greater autonomy in later phases as AI becomes more embedded. Throughout this process, AI reshapes skill requirements from routine to complex cognitive and adaptive skills. In the advanced phase of AI integration, we introduce the alternative paths and varied trajectories through which AI, organizational structures, and individual work experiences evolve. We conclude by discussing the implications of this framework for future research on AI and job design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Predictive Analytics in Employee Retention: A Decision Support Approach
items.abstract: Employee retention has become a strategic concern for commercial enterprises because avoidable turnover can increase recruitment costs, disrupt organizational knowledge, and weaken workforce continuity. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework linking artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource practices, predictive analytics capability, employee data quality, AI-supported career development, organizational support for AI, employee engagement, and employee retention. The framework follows a quantitative survey design and combines descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, multiple regression, mediation analysis, PLS-SEM-oriented measurement assessment, and machine-learning validation. A dataset of 250 responses is used only to demonstrate the structure and presentation of statistical analysis; it is not claimed to represent actual field observations. The results indicate acceptable internal consistency, positive associations among the principal constructs, significant predictive relationships, and stronger predictive performance for nonlinear machine-learning models than the regression baseline. The study positions AI and predictive analytics not as replacements for managerial judgement but as decisionsupport mechanisms for identifying retention risks, targeting interventions, and improving evidence-based workforce planning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Tool for Smart Policing
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) showed greater accuracy than traditional machine learning (ML) models for classifying crime incidents, particularly when the LLMs were fine-tuned using policing data. LLMs also showed greater accuracy in understanding the context and meaning of written crime reports, making crime analysis more efficient and accurate. All artificial intelligence (AI) technologies used for policing purposes should be implemented cautiously, with human oversight, transparency, and safeguards against biased training data to prevent discriminatory policing outcomes.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Research: A Critical Review of Current Developments, Challenges and Future Directions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been at the forefront of technological developments influencing business research. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled researchers to process increasingly complex data, automate analytical tasks and generate deeper insights. This study conducts a critical review of the evolution, applications, opportunities and challenges of AI in business research. Drawing upon contemporary literature from management, marketing, strategy, innovation, operations, finance and human resource management, the review synthesises knowledge regarding AI-driven decision-making, predictive analytics and knowledge creation. The review finds that AI improves research efficiency and supports evidence-based managerial decision-making. However, the literature highlights significant concerns relating to algorithmic bias, explainability, transparency, privacy, governance and research integrity. Existing scholarship is fragmented across disciplines and provides limited empirical evidence regarding the long-term implications of generative AI for research quality, organisational learning, governance effectiveness and human-AI collaboration. The study argues that AI should be viewed as a complementary capability that augments rather than replaces human expertise. By integrating evidence across multiple business functions, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps and develops a future research agenda focused on responsible governance, explainable AI and sustainable human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Evolving Roles of Teachers and Students in Human–AI Learning Ecosystems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force that is reshaping educational systems, pedagogical approaches, and learning environments. Similar to the impact of the Industrial Revolution on the development of mass education, the AI revolution has led to a fundamental reconsideration of educational objectives, teaching methods, curriculum structures, and the roles of teachers and students. Traditional educational models were largely teacher-centered and based on standardized curricula in which students acted as passive recipients of knowledge. In contrast, contemporary knowledge societies emphasize critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, problem-solving, and lifelong learning skills. In this context, AI technologies have accelerated the transition toward more learner-centered and personalized educational models. Subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, and big data analytics have increasingly entered educational environments through intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment tools, virtual assistants, and adaptive learning platforms. Applications such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Khan Academy’s Khanmigo illustrate the growing role of AI in teaching and learning processes. While these technologies provide significant opportunities for personalization, accessibility, and learning efficiency, they also raise ethical and social concerns related to data privacy, digital inequality, and academic integrity. This article systematically examines the historical and theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence in education and analyzes the evolving roles of teachers and students within AI-supported learning environments. Furthermore, the study evaluates the opportunities and challenges associated with AI integration and presents policy-oriented and practical recommendations for the ethical and effective implementation of AI technologies in education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration in Nursing Education: Perceived Barriers Among South African Nurse Educators and Nursing Students
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study investigates the perceived barriers to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into nursing education among nurse educators and nursing students at a public higher education institution in Gauteng, South Africa. Methods: A qualitative, exploratory, descriptive, contextual design was employed. Purposive sampling was used to recruit 12 nurse educators and 28 third-year nursing students. Data collection was conducted through semi-structured interviews with nurse educators and focus group discussions with nursing students. The data were analysed thematically, utilising Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework, with the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology(UTAUT) serving as an interpretative lens. Results: Four interrelated barriers emerged: infrastructure and resource constraints; limited AI literacy and skills; resistance and readiness challenges; and governance, ethical, and regulatory concerns. These barriers collectively influenced participants' willingness and capacity to engage with AI in nursing education. Conclusions: The effective integration of AI into nursing education necessitates coordinated institutional responses that address infrastructure, AI literacy, organisational readiness, and ethical governance. Developing contextually relevant policies, ensuring equitable access to technology, providing continuous professional development, and offering appropriate technical support may foster a more conducive environment for the responsible and sustainable integration of AI into nursing education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy and technology acceptance model-related constructs among first-year nursing students: a multi-institutional cross-sectional network analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence literacy is increasingly important in nursing education, but it remains unclear how its dimensions relate to three constructs related to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM): perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEU) and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (ATU). This study aimed to examine these relationships and to identify factors associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional study surveyed first-year nursing students at six undergraduate institutions in one province of China from 20 April to 1 May 2026. Of 375 questionnaire submissions, 362 met the quality-control criteria and were analysed (analytic retention rate: 96.5%). Separate item-level confirmatory factor analyses evaluated the four-factor literacy structure and the distinctiveness of PU, PEU and ATU. Group comparisons and multivariable regression with heteroscedasticity-robust inference examined correlates of overall artificial intelligence literacy; Pearson correlations described pairwise associations. A regularised partial correlation network mapped conditional relationships, centrality and bridge connectivity among seven dimension-mean nodes: knowledge, skills, values, ethics, PU, PEU and ATU. Between-institution differences, clustering and robustness of pooled findings were assessed. Results In the fully adjusted multivariable model, more frequent artificial intelligence use, prior artificial intelligence education and interest in artificial intelligence were positively associated with the mean artificial intelligence literacy score. The four-factor model showed good fit and strong item loadings; skills and values were highly correlated. Measurement analyses supported PU, PEU and ATU as correlated but distinguishable constructs. Of 21 potential network edges, 17 were non-zero. Skills had the highest expected influence and PU the highest strength. One-step bridge rankings were partition-dependent: values ranked first under the primary two-community partition and PU under the alternative four-community partition; PEU ranked second in both. Bootstrap diagnostics supported strong stability of strength and expected influence under case removal (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.751 for both). Intraclass correlation estimates were near zero; institution-adjusted analyses preserved the main regression and network findings. Conclusions Artificial intelligence use frequency, prior artificial intelligence education and interest were positively associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Skills, perceived usefulness, values and perceived ease of use may inform hypotheses for prospective evaluation of artificial intelligence education in undergraduate nursing programmes.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy, self‐efficacy and acceptance among nutrition and dietetics students, practitioners and academics: A cross‐sectional structural equation modelling study
items.abstract: AIM: To examine how artificial intelligence literacy, self-efficacy and perceptions and attitudes relate to artificial intelligence acceptance among nutrition and dietetics students, practising dietitians and academics in Türkiye. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 317 participants (98 undergraduate students, 139 dietitians, 80 academics) between February and August 2025 using validated scales. The model was tested with partial least squares structural equation modelling (5,000 bootstrap subsamples), specific indirect effects for mediation, and measurement invariance with permutation-based multi-group analysis. RESULTS: The model explained 56.4% of the variance in artificial intelligence acceptance. No structural path differed across the three groups after correction for multiple testing. items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven imaging-based prediction models for hemorrhagic transformation after mechanical thrombectomy in acute ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Objective Hemorrhagic transformation (HT) is a major complication after mechanical thrombectomy (MT) in acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven imaging-based prediction models have shown promise for predicting HT, their overall predictive performance remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated their predictive performance. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and CBM/SinoMed were searched from inception to July 2, 2026. Studies developing or validating AI-driven imaging-based prediction models for predicting HT after MT in AIS, including both pre- and post-procedural imaging predictors, were included. A random-effects model was used to pool the area under the curve (AUC), while a bivariate random-effects model was used to jointly estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity and construct the SROC curve. Subgroup analyses explored potential sources of heterogeneity. Results Eleven studies (total N = 3,541) were included, 10 studies contributed eligible AUC estimates, with evaluation cohorts ranging from 18 to 261 participants. The pooled AUC was 0.891 (95% CI: 0.853–0.928), with low between-study heterogeneity ( I 2 = 29.0%, p = 0.238). The bivariate random-effects model yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.666 (95% CI: 0.578–0.744) and a pooled specificity of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.842–0.960). Exploratory subgroup analyses did not provide robust evidence supporting the superiority of any specific subgroup, and their interpretation was limited by small subgroup sizes and methodological heterogeneity. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of studies within individual subgroups. Conclusion AI-driven imaging-based prediction models showed generally favorable discrimination in predicting HT after MT in AIS. However, current evidence does not establish the superiority of any specific model type. The predominance of retrospective studies, limited external validation, and methodological heterogeneity limit the generalizability of current findings. Large, multicenter prospective studies with rigorous external validation are needed before clinical implementation. Systematic review registration The systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261441463).

items.title: Assessing Workplace Technology Impacts on Employee Work and Wellbeing: A Post-Adoption Blind Spot
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly invest in adopting digital technologies to improve efficiency and competitiveness. Yet, in the post-adoption phase, these benefits depend on continued employee–technology interaction in everyday work, which can shape employee work and wellbeing and thereby influence organizational performance. Little is known, however, about how organizations assess these implications. Drawing on sociotechnical systems and performance measurement perspectives, this multiple-case study examines post-adoption assessment practices in eight Finnish organizations. The findings reveal a post-adoption blind spot: information on technology performance and use, employee work, and wellbeing was addressed through disconnected practices, indirect proxies, and informal judgements. Respondents reported recurring problems that remained weakly captured by current assessment: tool fragmentation, continuous adaptation demands, uneven performance effects, and work intensification, reflected more broadly in efficiency erosion and technology-related stress. The study conceptualizes integrated performance measurement systems as a potential mechanism for institutionalizing sociotechnical feedback through joint, recurring review of technology- and employee-related information.

items.title: Auditing the Product, Not the Recursion: The Evaluation Evidence Behind Recursive Self-Improvement Claims
items.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it.

items.title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
items.abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

items.title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
items.abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

items.title: CognitoShield AI: An Intelligent Platform for Digital Burnout and Cognitive Load Detection
items.abstract: Prolonged computer use can change the workload and strain a person experiences, but these changes are hard to see in task output alone. This paper presents CognitoShield AI, a privacy-oriented platform that estimates stress-related behavioral signals and cognitive workload indicators from interaction timing. The implemented pipeline aggregates telemetry into 30-second observations, derives a seven-feature representation, and applies an XGBoost regression model. A personal-baseline signal and a bounded context-aware fusion stage add personalization, and a FastAPI backend with a web interface presents the estimates together with recovery-oriented guidance. On a synthetic held-out test set, the model reached a mean absolute error (MAE) of 10.29, a root mean square error of 13.15, and an R-squared value of 0.7916. In an exploratory check of nine real users, the production seven-feature model recorded an MAE of 35.2367, while the P7 and P13 variants recorded 35.6300 and 35.2644, respectively. These results are preliminary and cannot establish generalization or clinical validity. The design does not collect raw typed characters and uses no camera-based or facial analysis. CognitoShield AI is therefore offered as a behavioral estimation and self-awareness tool, not a diagnostic system.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Pilot Workload in Dual-Pilot and Intelligent-Assisted Single-Pilot Operations
items.abstract: With the development of aviation automation and artificial intelligence, Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) have gradually become an important research direction for future civil aviation. Compared with conventional dual-pilot operations, SPO reduces the number of pilots in the cockpit, but the original flight tasks do not disappear. Instead, these tasks need to be redistributed among the single pilot, automated systems, and necessary ground support. Therefore, mitigating pilot workload arising from such task redistribution constitutes a key challenge for the development of SPO. Based on existing studies, this paper compares conventional dual-pilot operations with intelligent-assisted SPO, with particular attention to relatively high-workload phases such as approach and landing. The comparison focuses on three aspects: task distribution and quantity, task difficulty and time pressure, and task sequence and interaction. Through these dimensions, the paper examines how changes in crew configuration and task redistribution affect pilot workload and further discusses the role of intelligent assistance in workload management under SPO. The analysis suggests that the transition from dual-pilot operations to SPO primarily changes the distribution of tasks and workload. Without sufficient assistance, a single pilot may experience greater workload because more tasks can become concentrated on one person. Intelligent assistance can take over some monitoring, information-processing, and support functions, allowing tasks and attentional resources to be distributed more effectively. However, existing evidence remains insufficient to establish that intelligent assistance necessarily reduces the overall workload of SPO below that of conventional dual-pilot operations. Therefore, the development of intelligent-assisted SPO should focus on effective human–automation task allocation rather than simply increasing the level of automation.

items.title: Decolonising Generative Artificial Intelligence in African Higher Education: Toward Ubuntu-ẸkỌ, Augmented Collective Wisdom and Digital Sovereignty
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education presents both significant opportunities and critical challenges for institutions in Africa and the wider Global South. While GenAI can expand access to information, support teaching and learning, and strengthen research productivity, its deployment also raises questions concerning whose knowledge is represented, which languages are privileged, how credibility is constructed, and who exercises control over the infrastructures and data on which artificial intelligence depends. This article critically examined the implications of these challenges through the lenses of decolonial theory, epistemic justice, African philosophical thought, and critical AI studies. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a culturally neutral technological artefact, the article conceptualises AI as a sociotechnical system whose knowledge practices are shaped by historical, economic, linguistic and epistemological relations of power. Drawing on a critical interpretive synthesis of scholarly literature, policy documents and African philosophical perspectives, the article developed the Ubuntu-Ẹ̀kọ́ Framework as an original conceptual contribution. The framework brings together relationality, ethical character, contextual responsiveness, critical consciousness and communal capability. Building on this framework, the article proposes Augmented Collective Wisdom (ACW) as a reorientation of AI from a technology primarily designed to automate or individualise knowledge work toward a sociotechnical resource that supports collective learning, human judgement, cultural integrity and community wellbeing. The article further advanced Digital Sovereignty as a strategic alternative to a narrow discourse of AI readiness. It concluded that decolonising AI in higher education does not require rejection of technological innovation; rather, it requires institutions to develop the epistemic, cultural, linguistic, infrastructural and governance capacities necessary to determine how AI is designed, interpreted, deployed and evaluated within their own contexts.

items.title: Developing an AI Enabled Salutogenic Leadership Model for Abadan Oil Refinery
items.abstract: To develop a context-sensitive model of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled salutogenic leadership for Abadan Oil Refinery, integrating occupational well-being with the organizational requirements of digital transformation. This applied qualitative study integrated theoretical evidence with semi-structured interviews with 18 academic and organizational experts selected purposively for their knowledge of leadership, management, and AI applications. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed in ATLAS.ti using open, axial, and selective coding. Two independent coders reconciled disagreements through discussion; the reported Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. Preliminary categories were also reviewed by participating experts. The analysis generated 140 initial open codes and a six-category paradigm model. The model comprised causal conditions, intervening conditions, contextual conditions, strategies, a core phenomenon, and anticipated outcomes. Its core combined health-promoting and sustainable leadership, psychological coherence and occupational health, and readiness for human–AI collaboration. Causal conditions concerned leadership relationships, organizational and technological drivers, and attitudes toward technology. Contextual and intervening conditions encompassed health culture, job demands and resources, digital infrastructure, psychological capacities, and digital leadership. Strategies emphasized health support, stress management, leadership development, employee learning, and responsible technological adaptation. Anticipated outcomes concerned employee health and well-being, work attitudes and engagement, and sustainable organizational performance. The model frames AI as a resource for human decision-making within a health-promoting leadership approach. It provides an exploratory framework for refinery management rather than evidence that AI implementation improves health, safety, or productivity. The proposed relationships require prospective evaluation.

items.title: Empowerment of Islamic Religious Education Teachers through Generative AI Training for the Development of Islamic Value-Based Learning Media at SMP Negeri 35 Medan
items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, particularly Generative AI, has created new opportunities for developing innovative, interactive, and contextual learning media. However, many Islamic Religious Education (IRE) teachers still have limited competencies in utilizing this technology as a learning medium while maintaining Islamic values. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to improve the competence of IRE teachers at SMP Negeri 35 Medan in utilizing Generative AI to develop creative, effective, and Islamic value-based learning media. The program employed a Participatory Action Learning approach consisting of needs identification, educational sessions, practical training, mentoring, and evaluation. The training involved demonstrations and hands-on practice using various Generative AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Canva AI, Gamma AI, and Microsoft Copilot, to develop teaching materials, presentations, assessment questions, and visual learning media based on Islamic values. The results indicated an improvement in participants' understanding of Generative AI, enhanced skills in developing digital learning media, and increased awareness of the ethical use of AI from an Islamic perspective. The teachers were able to produce learning media that were more engaging, interactive, contextual, and supportive of the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum. This program contributed positively to improving teachers' digital literacy while strengthening the integration of technology and Islamic values in the IRE learning process.

items.title: Enhancing Adolescents' Physical Education Self Efficacy Through Artificial Intelligence Supported Feedback
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can provide individualized movement information at a frequency that is difficult to achieve through teacher observation alone. This study examined whether AI-supported corrective feedback could strengthen adolescents' physical education self-efficacy while improving movement execution. Eighty-four students aged 13–15 completed an eight-week controlled experiment involving bodyweight squats, forward lunges, and countermovement jumps. The AI group received pose-estimation-based feedback generated with MediaPipe Pose Landmarker and OpenCV, whereas the control group received standardized teacher feedback. The AI group increased self-efficacy from 4.17 ± 0.62 to 5.39 ± 0.56 points, compared with 4.19 ± 0.60 to 4.66 ± 0.61 in the control group, producing a significant group × time interaction, F(1,82) = 42.31, p < .001, ηp² = .340. Movement scores increased from 64.1 ± 6.8 to 82.3 ± 5.7 in the AI group. Within the AI condition, movement-score improvement and feedback engagement jointly predicted post-intervention self-efficacy, adjusted R²=.487. The findings indicate that interpretable, attempt-specific AI feedback can make mastery progress more visible and support both technical learning and efficacy beliefs in adolescent physical education.

items.title: Enhancing language learning with AI: the role of AI service quality in learning satisfaction and performance in mobile-assisted language learning applications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) applications are transforming the traditional language learning paradigm by leveraging AI technologies to provide a more efficient, convenient, and personalized learning experience. Despite the integration of AI technologies into MALL applications, prior studies have overlooked the critical role of AI service quality in shaping learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance within these applications. This study addresses this research gap by leveraging social support theory to develop a research model that examines how the AI service quality of AI-powered MALL applications influences social support, specifically informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support are further analyzed to determine their effects on learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance. A total of 978 valid samples were collected from users of AI-powered MALL applications and analyzed using the partial least-squares method. The results indicate that AI service quality significantly enhances users’ perceptions of informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support positively influence learning satisfaction and learning performance. Furthermore, the mediation analysis revealed that informational, emotional, and appraisal support act as partial mediators in the relationships between AI service quality and learning satisfaction and between AI service quality and learning performance. This study contributes to the literature by revealing how AI service quality, social support, and learning satisfaction and performance interact in the context of AI-enabled MALL applications. We also offer practical insights for improving the user experience and maximizing the learning outcomes of AI-driven MALL applications.

items.title: Enhancing the validity of probability prompts using four generative artificial intelligence tools
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) has become a large influence on students and teachers in the mathematics classroom. Specifically, researchers found that genAI tools could solve probability questions such as “What is the probability of drawing the Queen of Hearts from a standard deck of playing cards on the first try?” These researchers also stated that the genAI tools could not be trusted when solving, “Three cards are lying face down in front of me. Two are face cards, and there are no spades. No card is next to a card of the same color. What are the odds that the card on the left is the Queen of Hearts?” However, it is unclear whether that statement is true. Thus, we verified these findings by investigating four genAI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Co-Pilot, and Claude AI) on their ability to complete the identified probability task to determine when genAI can be trusted to perform probability calculation. Using the results of this investigation, we examined these genAI models using their responses and the predictions made by the genAI trainer. The investigation implies that developing mathematical validity requires intentional instruction, including teaching students how to compare genAI’s explanations, conducting GenAI Triangulation Process, cross-checking results using independent methods or alternative tools, and justifying whether an answer is mathematically sound.

items.abstract: This article aims to analyze the relevance of cognitive development and comprehensive ethical education in the critical and responsible use of generative artificial intelligence, with the purpose of preventing and counteracting the potential dehumanizing consequences that could affect the human condition in the twenty-first century. From a theoretical-analytical approach, it argues for the need for early digital education that fosters intellectual development and prevents technology from becoming a source of dependency. It highlights that education constitutes a key tool to counter cognitive laziness and the improper use of intelligent systems by university students, to the detriment of their critical reasoning capacities. It concludes that understanding the relevance of brain development and its relationship with cognitive learning processes constitutes an essential foundation for the formation of critical thinking and for the adoption of a responsible ethical approach to the use of artificial intelligence. Integrating these three components –cognitive development, critical thinking, and technological ethics—is indispensable for guiding the application of generative artificial intelligence toward pedagogical and humanistic ends that strengthen cognitive competencies, autonomy, and the reflective capacity of human beings in the twenty-first century.

items.title: Evaluating Generative AI Assisted Lesson Planning for Secondary Chemistry: A Critical Review of Planning Quality and Teacher Judgment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce chemistry lesson plans containing objectives, activities, resources, and assessments, but evaluating their educational contribution requires different kinds of evidence. This critical narrative review examines GenAI-assisted planning for secondary chemistry through three objects of evaluation: the written plan, teachers' professional reasoning and revisions, and students' learning. Seven recent chemistry and science education studies provide the principal contemporary evidence, interpreted alongside research on pedagogical content knowledge, chemical representations, and constructive alignment. The synthesis identifies useful planning support while showing why completed templates, teacher perceptions, and classroom outcomes require separate interpretation. Chemistry-specific review should examine the conditions attached to scientific claims, the connections among representations, the reasoning elicited by tasks, and the responses that trigger instructional adjustment. A worked illustration using electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate demonstrates how these criteria translate into changes to objectives, diagnostic questions, and follow-up teaching decisions. The article proposes a planning-review procedure and a teacher-education assignment that make justified revisions visible through planning records and discussion. Future studies can connect these records with classroom enactment and student explanations while separating AI assistance from additional opportunities to revise. The review positions teachers' transformation of generated materials as the link between the availability of planning support and the quality of the learning opportunities eventually offered to students.

items.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

items.title: Evolution of University Students’ AI Dependency and Creativity in the Technology Diffusion Process: A Four-Wave Repeated Cross-Sectional Study in China
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet potential risks accompany over-reliance on these tools. Grounded in Rogers’ diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. Four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (T1–T4, N = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. Key patterns emerged as follows: (i) Across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. The path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. Because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) AI-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the T1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (Δ = −0.391 to −0.549; d = −0.61 to −0.95; all p < 0.001 following Holm correction). This pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) The linkage between AI dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at T3 and became negative but non-significant at T4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. (iv) Observed wave-level differences for AI dependency and intrinsic motivation did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. Sensitivity tests yielded only two significant coefficients for AI dependency and none for intrinsic motivation; accordingly, these fluctuations are not given substantive theoretical interpretation. Retrospective qualitative accounts provided supplementary process-oriented context: participants reported initial exposure to AI driven by prevailing social trends, sustained use based on perceived utility, subsequent disappointment in unreliable or misleading outputs, and eventual shifts toward more strategic, self-regulated engagement. Given their retrospective nature, interview narratives were not used to triangulate or validate the quantitative findings. Collectively, this work suggests that as AI-supported learning becomes normalized within a diffusion-driven context, group-level indicators of students’ subjective creative experiences tend to decline. Higher-education institutions may therefore prioritize protecting learners’ creative agency as an explicit educational goal.

items.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
items.abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

items.title: Expertise modulates automation bias and sentinel behavior in human–AI collaborative diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum
items.abstract: Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.

items.title: Explainable AI for Detecting Safety Barrier Degradation from Near Miss Reports
items.abstract: Industrial maintenance generates near miss narratives that may reveal weaknesses in energy isolation, equipment integrity, permit coordination and other safety barriers. However, interpreting these reports requires contextual judgement, and an automated summary can conceal missing evidence or produce unjustified conclusions. This conceptual paper proposes an evidence-linked artificial intelligence framework for identifying reported barrier degradation and supporting accountable human review. The framework combines a controlled barrier taxonomy, source-linked extraction, retrieval from approved site documents, uncertainty handling and verification of corrective actions. Its central research proposition is that the value of AI should be evaluated through the quality of barrier decisions and the completeness of supporting evidence, rather than classification accuracy alone. A staged mixed methods protocol is specified, including expert annotation, temporal and site-separated testing, comparison with simpler methods, a randomised reviewer study and a prospective shadow deployment. Primary outcomes concern detection of expert-adjudicated barrier concerns, unsupported assertions and reviewer decision quality. Incident reduction is reserved for later investigation and is not inferred from report processing performance. No field dataset, implemented prototype or empirical results are presented. The contribution is a testable research design that connects explainable AI with practical safety assurance while retaining operational authority with competent personnel

items.title: Explainable Decision Graphs for Trustworthy Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are in-creasingly being considered for critical applications such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous transporta-tion. These systems consist of multiple intelligent agents that can independently perceive information, reason about their environment, communicate with other agents, and execute deci-sions. Although multi-agent architectures provide flexibility and scalability, their distributed decision-making process can make the overall system difficult to understand, audit, and verify. Existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) primarily fo-cus on explaining individual machine-learning predictions. They provide limited support for representing collaborative reasoning, inter-agent communication, conflicts, and collective decisions. This paper proposes an Explainable Decision Graph (EDG) framework for representing the reasoning process of autonomous multi-agent systems in a structured and interpretable form. The proposed framework models agents, observations, evi-dence, communications, intermediate decisions, conflicts, verifi-cation events, and final actions as interconnected graph com-ponents. A verification layer enables decision pathways to be examined against predefined safety and policy constraints. The resulting graph can provide different levels of explanations for end users, developers, and auditors. The paper defines an experimental methodology using multi-agent execution traces and proposes evaluation through ex-planation fidelity, completeness, decision traceability, human comprehensibility, decision accuracy, explanation consistency, and computational overhead. Empirical numerical results are intentionally reserved for the implementation and evaluation stage.

items.title: Financial self efficacy as a mediator of artificial intelligence use in detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks
items.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of financial self-efficacy in the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and the perceived effectiveness of detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks. The study addresses a behavioral and institutional gap in the literature by explaining how AI-supported monitoring capabilities may be translated into effective regulatory action through employees’ confidence in interpreting and using AI-generated outputs. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected from 115 employees working in compliance, Shariah compliance, Shariah supervision, internal audit, auditing, and risk management functions in Jordanian Islamic banks. The questionnaire consisted of 35 items measuring AI adoption, financial self-efficacy, perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness, and demographic characteristics. The data were analyzed using reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, standardized multiple regression, and regression-based mediation analysis. The results indicate that AI adoption has a statistically significant positive direct effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness after accounting for financial self-efficacy (β = 0.296, p = 0.001). AI adoption also has a significant positive effect on financial self-efficacy ( β = 0.640, p < 0.001), while financial self-efficacy has a significant positive effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness ( β = 0.491, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis shows a significant indirect effect of AI adoption on perceived detection effectiveness through financial self-efficacy (indirect effect = 0.314, Sobel z = 4.806, p < 0.001). The VAF value of 51.46% indicates complementary partial mediation. The findings suggest that AI adoption contributes to perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness not only through technological capabilities but also through employees’ financial self-efficacy. The study recommends integrating AI-supported monitoring systems with structured training, human-in-the-loop governance, and Shariah-sensitive regulatory procedures in Islamic banks.

items.abstract: Abstract There remains much more to Artificial Intelligence than understanding how to learn with neural networks. items.title: From AI labels to trust: cognitive pathways linking authenticity judgments, risk perception, and trust in AI-generated videos
items.abstract: Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.

items.title: From AI models to AI agents: governance through recursive oversight and revocable access
items.abstract: Recent developments in AI are shifting the main source of risk from the flawed outputs of individual models to the unintended effects of agentic AI systems. Limited but growing evidence of misaligned behavior in swarms of AI agents suggests that such systems can pursue unassigned tasks and act beyond the reach of traditional corporate governance tools, which presuppose agents with interests, fiduciary duties and legal personality. This paper argues that the object of governance should be expanded from the model in isolation to the agentic AI system as a whole, and that oversight should be calibrated to the combined level of capability, autonomy, external access, permissions and scale. It proposes a framework of recursive governance, in which monitoring, evaluation, intervention and authorization form a continuous feedback loop rather than a fixed checklist. Four propositions follow: (P1) governance must become more stringent as capability and operational autonomy combine with external access and scale; (P2) autonomous deployment at a given capability level should not occur unless predefined criteria for evaluation, monitoring, containment and independent verification are met; (P3) some governance functions should be embedded in the technical architecture rather than being left solely to ex post human intervention; (P4) enforcement should rest on conditional and revocable access to the infrastructure that autonomous operation requires, with the kill switch as the last resort of a broader regime, and should be anchored as far as possible to institutions, rules and forms of self-regulation that already exist. To this end, the paper proposes a three-stage enforcement architecture: (i) a lean, independent multilateral agency, composed mainly of experts in advanced AI, certifies that the governance process for AI agents is actually followed; (ii) the certificate is fully incorporated into the ESG framework already operating in the European Union and linked to existing EU legislation on sustainability reporting, sustainable finance and ESG ratings; (iii) the IMF includes AI governance compliance in its periodic surveillance of member countries through the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP). Apart from the new agency, which to our knowledge does not yet exist, enforcement would thus rely on institutions that are already in place. The proposed policies are framed as responses to three market failures: information asymmetry, negative externalities and a collective action problem among competing developers (a safety race to the bottom). The last of these is to be addressed through common safety standards, not through any relaxation of antitrust rules.

items.title: From AI-Assisted Performance to Independent Thinking: A Framework for Developing Higher-Order Thinking with Generative AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: In an AI-supported task, a student may explain a weak comparison once it has been identified, yet fail to notice a similar problem without a reminder. A decision about further help therefore needs evidence about what the student did without being prompted. We examine such decisions in English-medium university argumentation and evidence evaluation. The framework brings together English-language work on scaffolding, learner-generated reasoning, metacognitive calibration, and cognitive offloading. We distinguish help that supplies a reason from help that initiates a check. Readiness to work without the first does not establish readiness to work without the second. Coding examples and boundary cases make evidence about these functions interpretable, while six conditional propositions connect reconstruction and regulation to adaptation and transfer. A proposed experiment gives every group comparable diagnostic practice but varies whether teachers use its results to adjust assistance. This comparison isolates the value of using the evidence from learning through the diagnostic task itself. We relate the account to four GenAI approaches and illustrate it with a hypothetical sociology lesson. Help may be retained or restored when a new task requires it. The framework and coding rules need validation, particularly beyond the language and disciplinary settings considered here.

items.title: From disrupted routines to sustainable practice: integrating management sciences to navigate the innovation journey of precision imaging
items.abstract: Precision medicine is reshaping medical imaging through artificial intelligence, quantitative biomarkers or hybrid modalities such as PET-CT. Yet these tools reach patients unevenly, and that unevenness is usually blamed on technical problems: interoperability, validation, trust. Drawing on management science and the sociology of professions, we propose a different explanation. What decides whether an innovation reaches patients equitably is not the technology, but the way it travels. We distinguish three ways of travelling. Diffusion is spontaneous spread through professional networks (letting it happen). Dissemination is spread deliberately directed towards a defined population (helping it happen). Implementation is the work of turning an adopted innovation into everyday routine (making it happen). Imaging innovations have travelled mainly by diffusion, which follows existing specialist density, funding rules and like-with-like professional networks; diffusion therefore reproduces the inequalities of access it inherits instead of correcting them. Three consequences follow. First, adoption hides three separate decisions taken by different people: acquiring the equipment, deciding what the examination actually contains, and deciding whether it is requested at all. Routine statistics count the first and the third; the second is never measured. Second, professional boundaries are held in place at once by regulation, by specialty jurisdiction and by everyday working relationships, so reforms acting on only one of them fail. Third, the medical report is where those boundaries meet: when it does not carry an integrated answer, the innovation stalls. A fourth point runs through all three: an innovation's value is not fixed before it travels; its construction is predicated on the expectations that precede it, and the practices through which it is utilised. Using a three-study programme on PET-CT in France as illustration, we argue that equitable and sustainable precision imaging is achieved not by buying equipment but by governing how innovations spread—including by actively retiring the low-value practices they were meant to replace, what management science calls exnovation.

items.title: From joy to resistance: consumer reactions to disclosure of AI-created advertisements
items.abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that viewers tend to evaluate AI-generated advertisements negatively. We argue that viewers can nevertheless enjoy creative advertisements produced by AI. However, the belief that creativity is an exclusively human attribute may prompt cognitive regulation when AI involvement is disclosed. Using a consumer neuroscience approach, we conducted a one-factor, three-level between-subjects experiment in which participants viewed advertisements with no disclosure, disclosure of human–AI collaboration, or disclosure of full AI creation. Creative advertisements elicited joy, captured by facial expression analysis, regardless of whether they were created by humans or AI. Greater joy was associated with less message counterarguing and more favourable advertisement attitudes, but only in the absence of AI disclosure. These findings suggest that AI disclosure does not diminish initial enjoyment. Instead, it may act as a persuasion knowledge cue that activates cognitive regulation, leading viewers to override their positive affective responses when subsequently evaluating the advertisement.

items.title: From Prompting to Direct Manipulation: Interaction Patterns and Designer Experience in Generative AI-Supported Visual Workflows
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now employed in many visual design programs to create images rapidly, but these images may not meet the designer's expectations at first glance. This paper studies mismatch via text prompting, parameters and presets, reference-based input, and in-canvas manipulation. The fourteen academic sources in the review include thirteen peer-reviewed publications from 2024-2026 and Shneiderman's original work on direct manipulation. The workflow stage, participant group, interaction pattern, and the five dimensions of efficiency, perceived control, cognitive load, creative agency, and output predictability were used for evidence coding. Based on this evidence, the demand for refinement reduces the apparent advantage of rapid exploration. Effort saved in generation may be recovered by reducing prompt modifications, filtering output, or re-retrieving a suitable image. More local interactions help express and observe the decisions, but they do not eliminate the uncertainty in the generated results. Evidence for the parameters and presets is relatively scarce, so all four patterns cannot be evaluated equally. This framing clarifies how interface design, rather than model capability alone, affects professional agency and supports more informed tool selection in creative practice.

items.title: Future Machines on the Moon: Robotic Autonomy, Human Supervision and the Emerging Security Dimension of Lunar Operations
items.abstract: Lunar exploration has shifted from single flights to a planned buildup of permanent infrastructure. NASA flew four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II in April 2026, and within eight weeks announced the first three robotic Moon Base missions along with close to a billion dollars in contracts for surface rovers, cargo landers and hopping drones. A parallel programme led by China and Russia, the International Lunar Research Station, is working towards a basic configuration by 2035 with a nuclear power unit delivered between 2033 and 2035. This paper examines the machines that will carry out most of the work in both programmes. It sets out the supervised autonomy model that governs how humans and robots divide decisions under communication delay, identifies the specific artificial intelligence techniques that lunar robots depend on, and proposes an interaction protocol for surface operations. The paper then turns to security. Nearly every capability needed for lunar construction, survey and resource extraction has an obvious military application, and the argument advanced here is that any confrontation on the Moon would be short, machine-led and fought over access to a small number of usable sites rather than over territory in the terrestrial sense. Gaps in the Outer Space Treaty and in the Artemis Accords are assessed against that prospect.

items.title: Gamificación y motivación estudiantil: desafíos y oportunidades
items.abstract: Introduction: Gamification incorporates game design elements into educational activities and offers opportunities to strengthen student participation. However, its effects depend on planning, curricular objectives and implementation conditions. The aim was to analyse its relationship with student motivation and identify opportunities and challenges relevant to Ecuadorian upper secondary education. Methodology: A narrative review of twenty publications on motivational foundations, gamification and learning was developed, incorporating international contributions and a review situated in Ecuador. The synthesis addressed four dimensions: foundations, motivation, pedagogical opportunities and implementation challenges. Published findings were distinguished from teaching guidance derived from their interpretation. Results: The reviewed meta-analyses report favourable, although variable, effects on cognitive, motivational and behavioural outcomes. Evidence specifically concerning intrinsic motivation indicates a small effect, alongside improvements in autonomy and relatedness and a smaller effect on perceived competence. Feedback, progressive challenges and collaboration offer pedagogical possibilities, whereas controlling rewards, exclusionary competition, access barriers and assessment restricted to points require attention. Conclusions: Gamification can enrich teaching when game elements are linked to verifiable learning and inclusive participation opportunities. Its application to Ecuadorian upper secondary education requires contextual adaptation and assessment of understanding and sustained motivation. The narrative approach and diversity of sources limit generalisation and do not permit attribution of effects to specific institutions or causal conclusions about the Ecuadorian school context.

items.title: Generative AI and Social Inequality in Education: A Human-Centered Social Science Review of Global and Indonesian Evidence
items.abstract: This review examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can widen educational opportunity while also reproducing social inequality. An integrative review synthesized 24 sources: 17 Indonesian publications (2022–2026), identified through national journal portals and Google Scholar, and seven international policy documents and scholarly works (2016–2023) selected as conceptual anchors. Thematic analysis produced four themes: unequal access, unequal digital and AI literacy, unequal capacity to benefit from AI-supported learning, and governance risks involving privacy, bias, academic integrity, and human agency. The reported benefits of generative AI, such as tutoring, writing support, and translation, appear to depend on connectivity, devices, language resources, teacher competence, and students' ability to evaluate machine output. The Indonesian evidence is mostly cross-sectional, self-reported, or based on small single-institution samples, with little evidence on learning outcomes. One national household analysis of school participation (not AI use) found no significant difference between 3T (disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost) and matched non-3T households, suggesting that regional labels may be an imperfect proxy for household conditions. The review proposes a cumulative model of AI inequality that extends van Dijk's sequence of digital inequality with a governance stage and a feedback loop. The model is a conceptual proposition, not a tested result, and recommendations are ordered by the strength of supporting evidence.

items.title: Generative AI as a team moderator in CSCL : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
items.abstract: Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

items.title: Generative AI Driven Cultural Content Production Mechanisms and Creative Labor Substitution Effects
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping content production in the cultural and creative industries by shifting cultural material organization, script writing, exhibition interpretation, and cultural tourism communication from linear manual workflows to human-AI collaborative workflows. Focusing on productivity improvement and the boundary of creative labor substitution, this research constructs a three-group comparison framework involving human-only creation, AI-assisted creation, and fully AI-generated creation. Based on public cultural heritage data, cultural policy texts, and cultural tourism communication samples from 2018 to 2024, LLMs, RAG, Sentence-BERT semantic retrieval, expert scoring, and mixed-effects ANOVA are combined to measure generation quality, policy suitability, and substitution intensity across different cultural tasks. The results show that the average completion time of the AI-assisted group decreases from 44.2 min to 25.7 min, while the overall quality score increases from 82.6 to 84.1, indicating that human-AI collaboration can improve production efficiency while maintaining content quality. Although the fully AI-generated group achieves the lowest time cost, its policy suitability and cultural accuracy decline noticeably. Task complexity further affects substitution intensity. Cultural tourism copy and short-video scripts are more substitutable, while exhibition interpretation and policy explanation still rely on human judgment. These findings provide quantitative evidence for AI adoption, creative labor restructuring, and cultural policy governance.
